summary: Defines an XML Signature transform called XPath Filter 2.0. XML Signature lets part of an XML document be signed, and the original XPath transform can be hard to implement efficiently. This offers another way to pick the subset of a document to sign. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: You want to sign only part of a long letter. The old way of marking those parts was slow and clumsy. This is a smoother way to point at exactly the parts you want signed.

questions: how to sign part of an xml document
subtitle: A more efficient way to sign parts of an XML document

tldr.problem: XML Signature allows a subset of an XML document to be signed using the XPath transform, but evaluating XPath expressions for every node is slow and difficult to implement efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: XPath Filter 2.0 defines a new transform that evaluates a sequence of XPath expressions to identify subtrees, then combines them using set operations (intersection, union, subtraction) to select what to sign.
tldr.outcome: The new approach is significantly faster in practice because it avoids re-evaluating complex expressions for every node, making it practical for applications that need selective document signing.

today: RFC 3653 is an informational RFC that documents the W3C XPath Filter 2.0 Recommendation. It has not been obsoleted and remains the standard for efficiently filtering XML documents in digital signatures.

sections.title: Digital Signatures on Parts of Documents
sections.content:
XML Signature is a W3C standard that defines how to create and verify digital signatures in XML documents. One of its useful features is the ability to sign only a selected portion of an XML document rather than the whole thing. This is important for documents where some parts (like signatures themselves) should not be included when calculating the signature.

The original XML Signature specification includes an XPath transform that lets you specify which parts to sign by evaluating an XPath expression (a query language for XML). However, the standard approach of checking the XPath condition against every single node in the document proved slow and cumbersome to implement in practice. RFC 3653 introduces XPath Filter 2.0, a new transform designed to perform the same task much more efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine marking a chapter in a book for signing. The old way was to check every word to see if it matched your rule. The new way is to point at the chapter once and say sign that.

sections.title: How the Filter Works
sections.content:
XPath Filter 2.0 operates by building up a filter node-set (the set of nodes to be signed) through a series of XPath expressions combined with set operations. Instead of evaluating a condition against every node, it evaluates each XPath expression once to get a set of nodes, expands each result to include all descendant nodes, and then combines the results using intersection (keep only what is in both sets), subtraction (remove the matched nodes), or union (include matched nodes).

The filter starts with all nodes in the document. Each XPath expression is evaluated in sequence, and its result is combined with the current filter using the specified operation. Once all XPath expressions have been applied, the final filter node-set is used to select which nodes from the input will be included in the signature. This approach avoids the expensive operation of evaluating complex boolean expressions for every single node in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Start with all parts of the document. For each rule, find the matching parts and combine them using basic operations like add, remove, or keep-both. At the end, what is left is what you sign.

sections.title: Syntax and XML Structure
sections.content:
XPath Filter 2.0 is represented in XML using one or more XPath elements, each containing an XPath expression as character data. Each XPath element must have a required Filter attribute that specifies which set operation to apply: intersect, subtract, or union.

For example, to exclude a signature element itself from being signed, you would use: <XPath Filter='subtract' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2002/06/xmldsig-filter2'> here()/ancestor::dsig:Signature[1] </XPath>. The here() function refers to the XPath element itself, and the expression walks up the tree to find the containing Signature element.

When processing the transform, the XPath expressions are evaluated in the context of the document's root node, with context position and size both initialized to 1. A special function, here(), returns the XPath element that contains the expression, allowing filters to reference their own location in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: You write instructions like 'include this section' or 'remove that part' in a simple format. Each instruction has a keyword saying whether to add, remove, or keep only the matching parts.

sections.title: Common Use Cases
sections.content:
A frequent scenario is enveloped signatures, where a Signature element is nested inside the document it signs. The signature must not include itself in its own digest calculation. Using XPath Filter 2.0, you can express this as a single subtract operation that removes the Signature element and all its descendants from the signed content.

Another use case is co-signing, where multiple signatures are applied to the same document. With the intersect operation, you can specify that only a particular Signature element identified by an id attribute should be included in the new signature, while excluding all other content from the document.

A more complex example combines all three operations: intersect to select certain elements, subtract to exclude specific sub-elements, and union to re-include a deeply nested element that would otherwise be excluded. This is far more efficient to express and execute than trying to construct an equivalent single XPath expression and apply it to every node, as the original XPath transform would require.
sections.plainLanguage: Use cases include signing a document but not its own signature, signing one signature while excluding everything else, or signing sections of a document with complex exceptions.

sections.title: Implementation Efficiency
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that XPath Filter 2.0 can be implemented with a single pass through the document. Rather than expanding subtrees or explicitly performing set operations, implementations can maintain flags or counters to track whether each node is present in any union node-set, all subsequent intersect node-sets, and no subsequent subtract node-sets. If these conditions are met, the node is included in the output.

The RFC also notes that this computation can be efficiently combined with canonicalization processing, which is often the next step in signature calculation. This integration potential makes XPath Filter 2.0 particularly practical for real-world systems that need to sign selected portions of large XML documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The way it is built, computers can process it in one quick pass through the document, sometimes even at the same time as other steps they are taking.
